Research Proposal: Adaptive Difficulty Filtering for Domain-Specific Language
Model Pretraining## Title
AdaFilter: Adaptive Difficulty-Aware Data Filtering for
Domain-Specific Language Model Pretraining

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Domain-specific language models (e.g., BioBERT, CodeBERT, FinBERT,
Legal-BERT) are typically pretrained from scratch or continually trained on a
curated corpus of in-domain text. A critical but understudied bottleneck is how
to filter which documents from the domain corpus are actually useful for
downstream performance. Current practice relies on heuristics (perplexity
thresholds, hand-crafted rules, or simple length/n-gram filters) that are noisy,
domain-agnostic, and oblivious to the model's current state during training. The
result is wasted compute on low-quality or redundant documents and, in some
cases, performance degradation from noisy data.

Concrete gap: No existing method jointly models (a) document quality, (b)
difficulty relative to the model's evolving capabilities, and (c) domain
relevance in a unified, trainable filtering pipeline. Prior work treats these
dimensions separately or uses static filtering that does not adapt during
training.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
A trainable, difficulty-aware filtering module that scores documents
along three axes — domain relevance, linguistic quality, and current-model
difficulty — and dynamically selects a curriculum of documents during
pretraining will produce a domain-specific LM with better perplexity and
downstream task performance than static heuristic filtering, while reducing
total training tokens by ≥20%.

Null hypothesis: Adaptive difficulty filtering yields no statistically
significant improvement in downstream performance over static heuristic
filtering (perplexity, F1, or accuracy) when matched for total compute.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
We propose AdaFilter, a three-stage filtering framework integrated into
the training loop.

Stage1: Relevance Scoring (one-time preprocessing)

Use a small, efficient classifier (e.g., a FastText or MiniLM-based model) to
score each document against a set of domain-defining seed keywords or exemplars.
This is a lightweight binary classifier trained on a small hand-labeled set (~1K
documents per domain). Documents below a relevance threshold are discarded
before training begins.

Stage2: Quality Scoring (one-time preprocessing)

For surviving documents, compute three quality signals:

• Perplexity under a small reference LM (e.g., a125M-parameter general-domain
model) — anomalously high PPL flags gibberish.
• Repetition ratio — fraction of repeated n-grams (n=8).
• Information density — ratio of unique tokens to total tokens. Combine into a
scalar quality score via a learned linear weighting (trained on a held-out
quality-labeled set).

Stage3: Adaptive Difficulty Curricula (online, per-epoch)

During training, maintain a difficulty estimator — a small MLP that takes the
model's current token-level embeddings for the first K tokens of a document and
predicts a difficulty score. Documents are bucketed into Easy/Medium/Hard bins.
The training sampler draws:

• **Epoch1-2:**80% Easy,15% Medium,5% Hard (warm-up)
• **Epoch3-5:**40% Easy,40% Medium,20% Hard- **Epoch6+:**10% Easy,40%
Medium,50% HardThe difficulty estimator is updated every N steps to track the
model's evolving state.

Training Protocol- Continual pretraining (MLM objective) starting from a
general-domain checkpoint (e.g., RoBERTa-base).

• Compare against: (a) unfiltered data, (b) static perplexity-filtered data,
(c) random subset of equal size, (d) random subset of equal compute.
• Each condition is run with3 random seeds for statistical reliability.
• Downstream evaluation every5K steps using a held-out set of domain tasks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
We propose two domains for generalizability:

1 Biomedical: CORD-19 + PubMed abstracts (~2M documents). Downstream: BioASQ
(QA), ChemProt (RE), PubMedQA.
2 Legal: Pile-of-Law subset + EURLex (~1M documents). Downstream: CaseHOLD
(NLI), LexGLUE benchmark.

Each domain provides a clean test of whether domain-specific filtering matters
beyond generic heuristics.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Category | Metric | Target |

|---|---|---| | Language modeling | Validation perplexity | Primary | |
Downstream tasks | Macro F1 / Accuracy (domain-specific benchmarks) | Primary |
| Efficiency | Training tokens to match baseline best performance | Secondary |
| Curriculum effect | Per-bin difficulty distribution over epochs | Analysis | |
Ablation | Delta from removing each AdaFilter component | Diagnostic |

All metrics reported with95% confidence intervals across3 seeds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Description |

|---|---| | No Filter | All domain documents, no curation | | PPL Threshold |
Documents with PPL < median under general-domain LM | | Heuristic | Length +
n-gram repetition filter (common practice) | | Random Subset (size-matched) |
Same number of documents as AdaFilter, randomly sampled | | Random Subset
(compute-matched) | Same number of training steps as AdaFilter, randomly sampled
| | DSIR | Importance resampling using n-gram hashing (Xie et al.,2023) | |
FastText Relevance Only | AdaFilter Stage1 alone |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. No difficulty curriculum — Stage3 replaced with uniform sampling
from filtered pool → isolates curriculum contribution.

2 No quality scoring — Skip Stage2; only relevance + difficulty → isolates
quality signal.
3 Static buckets — Difficulty bins fixed at epoch1, never updated → isolates
benefit of adaptive difficulty.
4 Single domain — Run only on biomedical → tests domain transfer of findings.
5 Swap reference LM — Use a350M instead of125M reference model for perplexity →
tests sensitivity to reference size.
6 Score-to-weight variant — Instead of bucketing, weight documents by soft
difficulty score during loss → tests granularity benefit.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation |

|---|---| | Difficulty estimator collapses — becomes constant after a few epochs
| Add entropy regularization to bin assignment; monitor bin balance | |
Relevance classifier is the sole driver of gains (Stages2+3 add nothing) | If
ablation1 shows no degradation, the proposal still contributes an automated
relevance filter, which is a publishable result; reframe contribution around
end-to-end filtering | | Perplexity improves but downstream does not | Switch
primary evaluation to downstream tasks; analyze whether the LM is overfitting to
domain distribution at the expense of generalization | | High variance across
seeds | Increase to5 seeds; use paired bootstrap for significance testing | |
Adaptive curriculum underperforms static curriculum | Report honestly as
negative result with analysis of why — possibly because the domain corpus is too
homogeneous for curricula to matter | | Computational overhead of online
difficulty estimation outweighs token savings | Measure wall-clock time per1K
steps; if overhead >5%, treat as constraint and propose a cheaper proxy (e.g.,
loss on first128 tokens) | | Quality signals are highly correlated (redundant) |
Use PCA or mutual-information analysis on quality features; if redundancy is
high, the linear weighting in Stage2 will naturally down-weight correlated
features |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Success CriteriaThis proposal is considered successful if both conditions hold:

1 AdaFilter achieves statistically significant (p <0.05) improvement over all
baselines on at least one primary metric (perplexity or downstream F1) in
both domains.
2 AdaFilter uses ≤80% of the training tokens required by the best baseline to
reach the same downstream performance.

If only one domain shows gains, the contribution is domain-specific but still
publishable with the appropriate qualification.

Research Proposal: Structured Memory Banks for Long-Context Grounding in LLMs##
Title
Memory-Augmented Hierarchical Summarization (MAHS): Improving Long-Context
Grounding Without Full Attention Retraining

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Large Language Models suffer from the lost-in-the-middle problem — when
prompted with documents exceeding ~8K tokens, accuracy on facts located in the
middle of the context degrades sharply, even for models that claim128K+ context
windows. Two root causes: (1) softmax attention dilutes signal across many
tokens, and (2) positional encodings (RoPE, ALiBi) lose relative resolution at
extreme lengths. Existing solutions (ring attention, sparse attention,
state-space models) either require expensive full retraining or sacrifice recall
on mid-context facts.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Injecting a separately trained, retrieval-augmented memory bank —
built from hierarchically compressed chunks of the input context — into the
LLM's cross-attention layers will recover mid-context fact recall to within90%
of short-context performance without fine-tuning the base LLM. The memory bank
acts as a "second path" that bypasses diluted full-context attention.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
Component1 — Hierarchical Chunking & Summarization

• Split the input context into fixed-size chunks (e.g.,512 tokens each).
• For each chunk, generate a short natural-language summary (<=64 tokens) using
a lightweight LM (e.g., Phi-3-mini). This forms the first summary layer.
• Recursively apply the same process to the summary sequence to produce a
second, coarser summary layer.
• Store all chunks and summaries in a flat key-value store keyed by chunk
position and semantic embedding.

Component2 — Retrieval-Augmented Memory Attention

• Insert a small set of memory tokens (e.g.,128) at the start of each attention
layer's key-value cache during generation.
• At each decoding step, retrieve the top-k chunks/summaries (by cosine
similarity to the current hidden state) from the memory bank.
• Encode the retrieved chunks as additional key-value pairs appended to the
existing full-context KV cache for that layer, but with a separate learned
gating scalar that down-weights the full-context path when memory retrieval
has high confidence.

Component3 — Training (Lightweight)

• Freeze the base LLM entirely.
• Train only the memory encoder (a small transformer, ~50M params), the
retrieval projection layer, and the gating scalars.
• Training objective: next-token prediction on long-document perplexity, with
an auxiliary contrastive loss that pulls the hidden state closer to the
embedding of the chunk containing the ground-truth next token.

Base model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (128K context)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Benchmark | Purpose | Metric |

|-----------|---------|--------| | RULER (Hsieh et al.,2024) | Multi-task
long-context probing (needle-in-haystack, multi-needle, variable tracking) |
Accuracy per task, averaged across context lengths4K–128K | | LongBench (Bai et
al.,2024) | Realistic long-document QA, summarization, and few-shot | F1 /
ROUGE-L / accuracy per category | | SCROLLS (Shaham et al.,2022) | Long
narrative & legal document QA | F1 | | Custom: Mid-Context Perturbation Set | A
constructed50K-token corpus where every question's answer appears only in the
middle third (positions33%–66%) | F1 gap relative to same question with answer
in first10% |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics1. Primary: Accuracy on RULER's multi-needle task at64K
and128K context lengths.

2 Secondary:

• Perplexity on held-out long documents (16K–128K).
• Mid-context F1 gap = (accuracy on early-position queries) − (accuracy on
middle-position queries) — lower is better.
• Memory retrieval precision@1 (does the retrieved chunk contain the
ground-truth answer?).

3 Efficiency: Wall-clock time per generation token vs. baseline Llama-3.1 full
attention.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Why |

|----------|-----| | Base Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (full attention,128K) |
Reference point for lost-in-the-middle | | Llama-3.1 with chunked
cross-attention (no memory, no retrieval) | Ablates the retrieval component | |
LongLoRA fine-tune on long documents | Ablates the "no fine-tuning" claim | |
InfLLM (sparse attention + retrieval) | Closest published method; shows whether
memory bank approach improves over retrieval-only | | GraphRAG / MemWalker
(summarize-then-retrieve) | Tests whether hierarchical summarization alone
(without retrieval gating) is sufficient |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. No hierarchical summaries — flat chunk retrieval only. Tests whether
the summary hierarchy matters.

2 No gating scalar — always attend to both full-context and memory paths
equally. Tests whether the learned down-weighting is essential.
3 Memory bank size sweep —32,64,128,256 memory tokens. Characterizes the
trade-off between compute overhead and recall.
4 k retrieval sweep — top-1, top-3, top-5 chunks retrieved. Tests sensitivity
to retrieval depth.
5 Base model size — repeat best configuration on Llama-3.1-70B to test scaling
behavior.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation in Proposal |

|---|---| | Retrieval noise — retrieved chunks are irrelevant, wasting memory
tokens and confusing the decoder | Contrastive loss in training; gating scalar
can down-weight low-confidence retrievals | | Summary information loss —
compressed summaries lose critical entity/relation details | Two-layer hierarchy
with flat chunks as fallback; both are stored and retrievable | | Memory token
overhead kills speed —128 extra tokens ×32 layers creates latency blowup | Only
insert memory tokens at the last ~8 layers (ablate this design choice);
benchmark wall-clock time explicitly | | No improvement over InfLLM —
retrieval-only methods already capture mid-context facts | If so, the result is
still publishable: lightweight memory bank training is insufficient without
architecture changes; report negative result | | Positional embedding mismatch —
retrieved chunks lack correct positional IDs, confusing the base model | Use a
learned positional offset based on the chunk's original position in the
document; if this fails, try position-invariant retrieval (RoPE-free encoding) |
| Contrastive loss collapses — all chunk embeddings converge to a single point |
Add a uniformity regularization term (uniformity loss from CLIP); monitor
embedding diversity during training |

The research plan includes five objectives: implementing HiRASP in a LLaMA-2 backbone, training on a 32K-token corpus, evaluating on long-context benchmarks (LongBench, SCROLLS, L-Eval), performing ablation studies, and optimizing for efficiency. Expected contributions are a new hybrid architecture, an adaptive scaling mechanism, a dynamic internal retrieval method, empirical results showing state-of-the-art performance, and open-source implementations.

Research Proposal: Structured Memory Banks for Long-Context Grounding in LLMs##
Title
Memory-Augmented Hierarchical Summarization (MAHS): Improving Long-Context
Grounding Without Full Attention Retraining

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Large Language Models suffer from the lost-in-the-middle problem — when
prompted with documents exceeding ~8K tokens, accuracy on facts located in the
middle of the context degrades sharply, even for models that claim128K+ context
windows. Two root causes: (1) softmax attention dilutes signal across many
tokens, and (2) positional encodings (RoPE, ALiBi) lose relative resolution at
extreme lengths. Existing solutions (ring attention, sparse attention,
state-space models) either require expensive full retraining or sacrifice recall
on mid-context facts.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Injecting a separately trained, retrieval-augmented memory bank —
built from hierarchically compressed chunks of the input context — into the
LLM's cross-attention layers will recover mid-context fact recall to within90%
of short-context performance without fine-tuning the base LLM. The memory bank
acts as a "second path" that bypasses diluted full-context attention.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
Component1 — Hierarchical Chunking & Summarization

• Split the input context into fixed-size chunks (e.g.,512 tokens each).
• For each chunk, generate a short natural-language summary (<=64 tokens) using
a lightweight LM (e.g., Phi-3-mini). This forms the first summary layer.
• Recursively apply the same process to the summary sequence to produce a
second, coarser summary layer.
• Store all chunks and summaries in a flat key-value store keyed by chunk
position and semantic embedding.

Component2 — Retrieval-Augmented Memory Attention

• Insert a small set of memory tokens (e.g.,128) at the start of each attention
layer's key-value cache during generation.
• At each decoding step, retrieve the top-k chunks/summaries (by cosine
similarity to the current hidden state) from the memory bank.
• Encode the retrieved chunks as additional key-value pairs appended to the
existing full-context KV cache for that layer, but with a separate learned
gating scalar that down-weights the full-context path when memory retrieval
has high confidence.

Component3 — Training (Lightweight)

• Freeze the base LLM entirely.
• Train only the memory encoder (a small transformer, ~50M params), the
retrieval projection layer, and the gating scalars.
• Training objective: next-token prediction on long-document perplexity, with
an auxiliary contrastive loss that pulls the hidden state closer to the
embedding of the chunk containing the ground-truth next token.

Base model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (128K context)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Benchmark | Purpose | Metric |

|-----------|---------|--------| | RULER (Hsieh et al.,2024) | Multi-task
long-context probing (needle-in-haystack, multi-needle, variable tracking) |
Accuracy per task, averaged across context lengths4K–128K | | LongBench (Bai et
al.,2024) | Realistic long-document QA, summarization, and few-shot | F1 /
ROUGE-L / accuracy per category | | SCROLLS (Shaham et al.,2022) | Long
narrative & legal document QA | F1 | | Custom: Mid-Context Perturbation Set | A
constructed50K-token corpus where every question's answer appears only in the
middle third (positions33%–66%) | F1 gap relative to same question with answer
in first10% |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics1. Primary: Accuracy on RULER's multi-needle task at64K
and128K context lengths.

2 Secondary:

• Perplexity on held-out long documents (16K–128K).
• Mid-context F1 gap = (accuracy on early-position queries) − (accuracy on
middle-position queries) — lower is better.
• Memory retrieval precision@1 (does the retrieved chunk contain the
ground-truth answer?).

3 Efficiency: Wall-clock time per generation token vs. baseline Llama-3.1 full
attention.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Why |

|----------|-----| | Base Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (full attention,128K) |
Reference point for lost-in-the-middle | | Llama-3.1 with chunked
cross-attention (no memory, no retrieval) | Ablates the retrieval component | |
LongLoRA fine-tune on long documents | Ablates the "no fine-tuning" claim | |

memory bank approach improves over retrieval-only | | GraphRAG / MemWalker
(summarize-then-retrieve) | Tests whether hierarchical summarization alone
(without retrieval gating) is sufficient |

the summary hierarchy matters.

equally. Tests whether the learned down-weighting is essential.

behavior.

|---|---| | Retrieval noise — retrieved chunks are irrelevant, wasting memory
tokens and confusing the decoder | Contrastive loss in training; gating scalar

with flat chunks as fallback; both are stored and retrievable | | Memory token

benchmark wall-clock time explicitly | | No improvement over InfLLM —

Title: CULTURAL-PREF: Preference Tuning with Culturally-Grounded Contrastive
Examples for Cross-Cultural LLM AlignmentProblem. Current RLHF/DPO alignment
pipelines overwhelmingly use preference data annotated by English-speaking,
Western raters. This produces models that (a) treat Western cultural norms as
universal defaults, (b) give culturally inappropriate or offensive answers in
non-Western contexts, and (c) lack measurable mechanisms to control which
cultural frame the model should adopt for a given user or query. No existing
work has systematically decomposed which dimensions of alignment (helpfulness,
harmlessness, honesty, social norms) are most culturally divergent, nor tested
whether targeted preference data can close the gap without degrading Western
performance.

Hypothesis. Fine-tuning an LLM with preference pairs where the same query
receives different culturally appropriate responses across target cultures
(e.g., Japanese vs. Brazilian vs. Saudi Arabian social norms) will produce a
model whose outputs can be steered toward a specified cultural frame via a
lightweight prompt prefix, while maintaining competitive performance on standard
Western-centric benchmarks. The core claim: cultural divergence in alignment is
concentrated in a small set of behavioral dimensions (social hierarchy,
indirectness, taboo topics, gift-giving norms, and individualist vs.
collectivist framing), and targeted contrastive examples on these dimensions
suffice to induce generalizable cross-cultural behavior.

Method. Three-stage pipeline:

1 Taxonomy construction. Use a research-agent-assisted literature review of
cross-cultural psychology (Hofstede dimensions, GLOBE project, Hall's
high/low context) and existing culturally-aware LLM datasets (CULTURALBENCH,
CULTUREPAIR, GLOBALALIGN) to produce a taxonomy of8–12 behavioral dimensions
where LLM outputs are expected to diverge across cultures. Each dimension
gets a one-paragraph annotation specifying the expected range of appropriate
behavior.
2 Contrastive preference dataset. For each dimension, generate200–400
query-response triples (query, culturally-appropriate-response-A,
culturally-appropriate-response-B) across two target cultures (e.g.,
US-English and Japanese) using human annotation or validated LLM-as-judge
pipelines with culture-specific rubrics. Each triple explicitly labels which
cultural frame each response fits. Total target: ~3,000–5,000 preference
pairs.
3 Preference tuning & steering. Fine-tune a base model (e.g., Llama-3-8B or
Qwen-2.5-7B) via DPO on the contrastive dataset. Add a steering mechanism: a
prepended system prompt specifying the target cultural frame (e.g., "You are
a helpful assistant responding to someone in Japan. Follow Japanese social
norms: use polite register, avoid direct refusals, respect hierarchical
address."). Evaluate whether steering via prompt alone suffices or whether a
lightweight adapter (LoRA per culture) is needed.

Dataset / Benchmark.

• Training: Custom constructed dataset (described above).
• Evaluation: CULTURALBENCH (cross-cultural QA and social norms), CULTUREPAIR
(culturally sensitive comparison pairs), and a subset of GLOBALALIGN (moral
and social alignment across10+ countries). Also construct a held-out
"cross-cultural adversarial" test set of200 prompts where the appropriate
response differs sharply between two cultures (e.g., feedback to a superior,
gift refusal, discussion of religious holidays).

Evaluation Metrics.

• Cultural appropriateness score: Agreement with human raters from each target
culture (≥3 raters per item, Krippendorff's α ≥0.7 threshold) on a5-point
Likert scale measuring whether the response is culturally appropriate for the
specified frame.
• Steerability accuracy: For each culture-steered query, does the model's
response align with the intended culture (vs. default/majority culture)?
Measured by both human evaluation and an LLM judge fine-tuned on the same
taxonomy.
• Western benchmark retention: Performance drop on HellaSwag, MMLU, and
MT-Bench. Threshold: ≤2% absolute degradation.
• Dimension-level divergence: Per-dimension score showing which cultural
dimensions the model handles well vs. poorly.

Baselines.

1 Base model (no fine-tuning): Shows the default cultural bias of the
pretrained model.
2 Standard DPO (general preference data): Trained on the full HelpSteer2 or
UltraFeedback dataset (no cultural conditioning). Measures whether standard
alignment already produces monocultural outputs.
3 Naive prompt steering: Apply the same culture-steering prompt to the base
model without fine-tuning. Isolates the effect of prompting vs. preference
tuning.
4 Culture-agnostic DPO + prompt steering: DPO on the contrastive dataset
without culture labels during training, but with steering prompts at
inference. Tests whether contrastive data alone helps even without labeled
training.

Ablations.

• Dimension ablation: Remove one behavioral dimension at a time from the
contrastive dataset. Which dimensions are critical for cross-cultural
generalization?
• Data scaling: Train on10%,25%,50%,100% of the contrastive dataset. Is there a
diminishing-returns threshold?
• Model scale: Repeat the best configuration on a1B,7B, and27B parameter model
(or whatever sizes are available). Does cross-cultural steerability scale
with model size?
• Target culture ablation: Train on US–Japan pairs only, then evaluate on
US–Brazil and US–Saudi Arabia. Does the method generalize to unseen target
cultures?

Expected Failure Modes.

1 Surface-level mimicry. The model learns to insert polite markers and
culture-specific keywords without understanding deeper social norms (e.g.,
produces Japanese honorifics but gives a direct refusal that violates
Japanese indirectness norms). Mitigation: Include examples where the surface
form and deep norm diverge, and evaluate with adversarial probes that test
for this distinction.
2 Steering interference. The culture-steering prompt competes with the base
model's pre-existing alignment (refusal training, safety filters), producing
unpredictable behavior in safety-critical queries. Mitigation: Explicitly
include edge-case safety prompts in the contrastive dataset and measure
safety metric separately.
3 Overfitting to stereotype. The taxonomy-based approach encodes stereotypical
or outdated cultural norms, producing responses that caricature rather than
respect the target culture. Mitigation: Validate all dimension annotations
with in-culture reviewers; include intra-cultural variation examples (e.g.,
both formal and informal Japanese responses).
4 Western performance collapse. Teaching the model to deviate from its default
alignment causes broad degradation on standard English benchmarks.
Mitigation: Monitor Western benchmarks throughout training, early-stop if
degradation exceeds2%, and test whether a residual connection or adapter
merging strategy preserves base capabilities.
5 Rater disagreement. Human raters from the same culture disagree on what
constitutes an appropriate response, making the ground-truth labels noisy.
Mitigation: Use an agreement threshold (Krippendorff's α ≥0.7) and discard or
re-annotate items below it. Report confidence intervals on all human
evaluation metrics.
6 Non-transferability to unseen cultures. The model learns a mapping from
"culture token → behavior" but fails on cultures not seen during training.
Mitigation: The target-culture ablation (train on US–Japan, test on
US–Brazil, US–Saudi Arabia) directly tests this; if it fails, the method
collapses to a retrieval problem rather than actual cultural generalization.

Research Proposal: Steering Vector–Based Value Control in Large Language
Models## Title
Value Steering Without Fine-Tuning: Representation Engineering for
Controllable AI Alignment

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current value alignment methods for LLMs — primarily RLHF and
constitutional AI — operate at the parametric level: they fine-tune model
weights using reward-model scores or self-critique data. This creates two
unresolved problems:

1 Value brittleness under distribution shift — an RLHF-tuned model may behave
consistently on in-distribution helpfulness/harmlessness prompts but fail on
adversarial inputs, domain shifts, or tasks that were not represented in the
preference data.
2 Value entanglement with capability — fine-tuning for alignment inevitably
modifies weights that also encode reasoning, factual recall, and linguistic
ability, making it difficult to attribute behavior changes to "value
learning" versus capability degradation or surface-level pattern matching.

A method that can separately control value-relevant behavior without modifying
base weights would enable testable hypotheses about whether alignment is a
representational property or a learned behavioral policy.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Primary hypothesis: For a given LLM, there exists a low-dimensional
subspace in the residual stream (or attention head outputs) such that
intervention along a value direction — defined by contrasting activation
patterns on value-consistent vs. value-violating examples — shifts the model's
alignment-relevant generation behavior on held-out prompts with statistical
significance (p <0.01, Bonferroni-corrected across5 dimensions) while preserving
perplexity on standard language modeling benchmarks within2% of the unmodified
model.

Secondary hypothesis: Value steering vectors generalize across related value
dimensions (e.g., a "honesty" vector improves "fairness" behavior) but are
separable from capability-related vectors (e.g., "reasoning quality," "factual
recall"), as measured by cosine similarity between steering directions <0.15.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
The proposal adapts representation engineering (RepE) (Zou et al.,2023) to
value alignment with three modifications:

1 Contrastive activation collection. For each target value dimension (e.g.,
helpfulness, harmlessness, honesty, fairness), collect500 contrast pairs from
a public preference dataset (Anthropic HH-RLHF or PKU-SafeRLHF). Each pair
consists of a value-consistent completion and a value-violating completion
for the same prompt. Extract hidden states at every layer from the residual
stream and attention outputs for both completions. The value direction for
layer l is the top PCA component of the difference vectors Δ = h(consistent)
− h(violating).
2 Reading and steering. Two operations:

• Reading: Compute alignment along each direction for a test prompt by
projecting the model's activations onto the value direction. This produces a
scalar "value alignment score" per layer without any generation.
• Steering: At inference time, add a scaled value direction vector (coefficient
α) to the residual stream at a chosen layer set. Generate completions under
steering. Vary α ∈                                                           Goodbye!

depth, or patch size?

hybrid objective that combines masked reconstruction with a contrastive
alignment loss (audio-text), testing the hypothesis that reconstruction alone is
insufficient for general-purpose transfer.

yields representations that transfer to speech, music, and environmental tasks
as well as or better than a hybrid reconstruction + contrastive objective.

during pretraining significantly improves downstream transfer on tasks requiring
high-level semantics (e.g., audio captioning, zero-shot sound classification),
while maintaining or improving performance on acoustic-only tasks (e.g., scene
classification).
